v2.rule: In a main clause the conjugated verb is always in second place. In these sentences the subject comes first: subject – verb – rest. If you put a place or a time at the start, the subject moves after the verb.

items.it: I work in Brussels.
items.e: Subject ik, then the verb werk in 2nd place, then the place.

items.it: My sister lives in Ghent.
items.e: Mijn zus is a single block (the subject), so woont is still in 2nd place.

items.it: I'm having a coffee.
items.e: Subject – verb – object, just like in English.

items.it: My father reads the newspaper.
items.e: The verb leest comes right after the subject, the object after the verb.

items.it: We speak Dutch.
items.e: Wij is the subject; the verb is in 2nd place.

items.it: The children are playing in the garden.
items.e: Subject (two words, one block) – verb – place. Dutch has no -ing form: spelen covers both “play” and “are playing”.

items.it: Our apartment is very nice.
items.e: is is a conjugated verb too: 2nd place.

items.it: The train is late.
items.e: Subject – verb – rest: te laat closes the sentence.

items.it: The store closes at six.
items.e: The verb sluit in 2nd place; if you put the time first, the subject goes after the verb.

items.it: Marc gives his mother flowers.
items.e: Verb in 2nd place; without aan, the person (zijn moeder) comes before the thing (bloemen), as in English.

inv.rule: If the sentence starts with a time or a place, the verb stays in 2nd place and the subject goes after the verb: time/place – verb – subject – rest. The first block is already in place.

items.it: Tomorrow I'm going to Ghent.
items.e: Morgen takes 1st place, so ga comes next and then ik. Unlike English, not Morgen ik ga.

items.it: My aunt lives in Ghent.
items.e: Place at the start → verb → subject.

items.it: Today I'm working from home.
items.e: After vandaag the verb comes right away, then the subject ik.

items.it: Tonight we're cooking pasta.
items.e: Inversion: koken we, not we koken.

items.it: On Saturdays we go to the market.
items.e: Time in 1st place, verb in 2nd, subject in 3rd.

items.it: After work I have a beer.
items.e: Na het werk is one element, so the verb follows it. (Een pintje = a beer, in Belgium.)

items.it: At eight o'clock the class starts.
items.e: Time at the start → begint → subject.

items.it: In the summer we often go to the seaside.
items.e: Verb, subject, then the adverb vaak before the place.

items.it: Every day my son bikes to school.
items.e: Verb, subject, then manner (met de fiets) before place (naar school).

items.it: Tomorrow morning my mother is calling the doctor.
items.e: After the time: the verb belt, the subject, the object.

tmp.rule: After the verb, information usually follows the order time – manner – place: Ik ga morgen met de trein naar Gent. English often does the opposite (“to Ghent by train tomorrow”). The subject is already in place.

items.it: I'm going to Ghent tomorrow.
items.e: First the time (morgen), then the place (naar Gent).

items.it: We're eating at home tonight.
items.e: Time before place: vanavond thuis.

items.it: My brother bikes to work.
items.e: Manner (met de fiets) before place.

items.it: I'm going to Ghent by train tomorrow.
items.e: Time – manner – place: morgen – met de trein – naar Gent.

items.it: She works in Brussels every day.
items.e: The time (elke dag) comes before the place.

items.it: He comes to the office by bus at nine.
items.e: Time – manner – place, the reverse of the usual English order.

items.it: On Saturday we're going to the seaside with friends.
items.e: When (zaterdag), with whom/how (met vrienden), where (naar zee).

items.it: Today my parents are driving to Antwerp.
items.e: Time – manner – place: vandaag – met de auto – naar Antwerpen.

items.it: My sister cycles in the park every morning.
items.e: Time before place.

items.it: Tomorrow at eight the children are taking the bus to school.
items.e: General time before precise time (morgen om acht uur), then manner and place.

q.s: Verb first, or after the question word
q.rule: Yes/no question: the verb goes in 1st place: Woon je in Gent? With a question word: question word – verb – subject – rest: Waar woon je? Dutch never uses a helper like English do. With je/jij after the verb, the -t drops.

items.it: Do you live in Ghent?
items.e: Yes/no question: verb in 1st place, no do. Woon je, without -t.

items.it: Do you speak French?
items.e: Verb, subject, rest.

items.it: Do you have a garden?
items.e: The verb heb opens the question.

items.it: Where do you live?
items.e: Question word, then the verb right away, then the subject.

items.it: What are you drinking?
items.e: Wat in 1st place, verb in 2nd.

items.it: What's your brother's name?
items.e: Question word – verb – subject: literally “How is your brother called?”.

items.it: How much does the cheese cost?
items.e: Hoeveel, then the verb, then the subject.

items.it: Are you working from home tomorrow?
items.e: Verb in 1st place; after the subject, time before place.

items.it: When are you (all) going to Bruges?
items.e: Question word – verb – subject – rest. jullie = you (plural).

items.it: Why are you learning Dutch?
items.e: Waarom leer je: verb in 2nd place, subject right after.

mod.s: The infinitive goes at the end
mod.rule: The modal verb (willen, kunnen, moeten, mogen) is conjugated and sits in 2nd place; the infinitive goes to the end: Ik wil koffie drinken. Everything else goes in between — unlike English, where the two verbs stay together.

items.it: I want to drink coffee.
items.e: wil in 2nd place, drinken at the end. No “to” in Dutch after a modal.

items.it: You're allowed to park here.
items.e: Modal in 2nd place, infinitive at the end; hier goes in between (or at the start, with inversion).

items.it: We have to work tomorrow.
items.e: werken goes to the end, after morgen.

items.it: Can you help me?
items.e: Question: modal in 1st place, infinitive always at the end.

items.it: He can cook well.
items.e: kan in 2nd place, koken at the end, the adverb in between.

items.it: My sister wants to live in Antwerp.
items.e: The place goes in between, wonen closes the sentence.

items.it: We want to buy a new bike.
items.e: The object in between, the infinitive kopen at the end.

items.it: You're not allowed to smoke here.
items.e: niet goes right before the final infinitive.

items.it: Tonight I have to clean the kitchen.
items.e: poetsen (to clean, in Belgium) goes to the end; everything else sits between the modal and the infinitive.

items.it: When can we go to Ghent?
items.e: Question word, modal, subject… and gaan at the end.

sep.s: The particle goes at the end
sep.rule: With separable verbs (opstaan, opbellen, meenemen) the conjugated part is in 2nd place and the particle goes to the end: Ik sta om zeven uur op — a bit like English “I get up”, but the particle goes all the way to the end. With a modal the verb stays whole at the end: Ik moet vroeg opstaan.

items.it: I get up at seven.
items.e: opstaan: sta in 2nd place, op at the end.

items.it: The train arrives at ten.
items.e: aankomen: the particle aan closes the sentence.

items.it: I'm calling my mother.
items.e: opbellen: the object sits between bel and op, like “call my mother up”.

items.it: He's taking an umbrella with him.
items.e: meenemen: neemt … mee.

items.it: We're going out tonight.
items.e: uitgaan: uit at the end, even after the time.

items.it: When are you coming back?
items.e: terugkomen: in questions too, the particle goes to the end.

items.it: The store opens at nine.
items.e: opengaan: gaat … open.

items.it: I have to get up early tomorrow.
items.e: With the modal moet, the separable verb stays whole at the end: opstaan.

items.it: Can you call me tomorrow?
items.e: Modal first (question), opbellen whole at the end; the pronoun me right after the subject.

items.it: I don't want to go out tonight.
items.e: niet before the infinitive, which stays whole: uitgaan.

perf.s: The participle goes at the end
perf.rule: The auxiliary (hebben or zijn) is conjugated and sits in 2nd place; the past participle goes to the end: Ik heb koffie gedronken. Everything else goes in between. Dutch uses this tense where English often uses the simple past (“I drank”).

items.it: I drank a coffee.
items.e: heb in 2nd place, gedronken at the end.

items.it: We went to Bruges.
items.e: With gaan the auxiliary is zijn; the participle closes the sentence.

items.it: He worked yesterday.
items.e: gisteren goes in between (or at the start, with inversion), gewerkt at the end.

items.it: What did you eat?
items.e: Question word, auxiliary, subject, participle.

items.it: My parents bought a new house.
items.e: The object sits between hebben and gekocht.

items.it: She left at eight.
items.e: vertrekken takes zijn; the participle goes to the end.

items.it: Have you read the newspaper?
items.e: Question: auxiliary in 1st place, participle always at the end.

items.it: Yesterday I stayed home.
items.e: Time before place, and gebleven at the end.

items.it: We ate fries in Ghent.
items.e: The participle gegeten at the end; frieten stays close to the verb.

items.it: Last year I traveled to Italy by train.
items.e: Time – manner – place in between, the participle gereisd at the end.

niet.s: After the object, before the rest
niet.rule: niet goes after the conjugated verb and a definite object (Ik ken hem niet), but before an adjective, a preposition, an infinitive or a participle: Ik ben niet moe, Hij woont niet in Gent. There is no helper verb like English don't.

items.it: I'm not tired.
items.e: niet before the adjective.

items.it: My sister doesn't smoke.
items.e: With nothing after it, niet goes at the end, after the verb. No “does” in Dutch.

items.it: I don't know him.
items.e: niet after the definite object hem.

items.it: I don't understand it.
items.e: The pronoun het comes before niet.

items.it: The soup isn't hot.
items.e: niet before the adjective warm.

items.it: He doesn't live in Ghent.
items.e: niet before the preposition in.

items.it: We're not taking the car.
items.e: niet after the definite object de auto.

items.it: I can't come today.
items.e: niet before the infinitive, after the time.

items.it: We're not going to school tomorrow.
items.e: niet after the time and before naar school.

items.it: I didn't find it.
items.e: Object het, then niet, then the participle at the end.

sub.s: The verb goes at the end
sub.rule: After omdat, dat, als, of, wanneer (and waar in indirect questions) a subordinate clause begins: the conjugated verb goes to the end: …omdat het regent, …dat hij ziek is. The main clause stays normal: verb in 2nd place. English keeps the same order in both, so this takes practice.

items.it: I'm staying home because it's raining.
items.e: After omdat the verb regent goes to the end of the clause.

items.it: I think he's sick.
items.e: dat hij ziek is: verb at the end, not dat hij is ziek. Unlike English “that”, dat can't be left out.

items.it: She says the soup is cold.
items.e: In the dat clause the verb is goes to the end.

items.it: Do you know if the store is open?
items.e: of = if/whether: here too the verb goes to the end.

items.it: We're going to the park if the weather is nice.
items.e: als het mooi weer is: verb at the end of the clause.

items.it: Marc isn't coming because he's tired.
items.e: Normal main clause (komt in 2nd place), subordinate clause with the verb at the end.

items.it: I don't know where he lives.
items.e: Indirect question with waar: woont goes to the end.

items.it: Call me when you're home.
items.e: Imperative first; after wanneer the verb bent goes to the end.

items.it: She's asking whether we're coming tomorrow.
items.e: of we morgen komen: subject, time, verb.

items.it: I hope it doesn't rain tomorrow.
items.e: In the subordinate clause niet goes right before the final verb.

want.rule: want and omdat both mean “because”. After want the order is normal (verb in 2nd place): want het is koud. After omdat the verb goes to the end: omdat het koud is. Only the omdat clause can go at the start of the sentence.

items.it: We're staying home, because it's raining.
items.e: After want: subject – verb, like a normal sentence.

items.it: We're staying home because it's raining.
items.e: After omdat the verb goes to the end (here it matches the want order, since there's only the verb).

items.it: I'm taking a jacket, because it's cold.
items.e: want het is koud: verb in 2nd place.

items.it: I'm taking a jacket because it's cold.
items.e: omdat het koud is: verb at the end.

items.it: Anna isn't eating anything, because she isn't hungry.
items.e: After want: ze heeft, normal order.

items.it: Anna isn't eating anything because she isn't hungry.
items.e: After omdat: heeft at the end.

items.it: I'm learning Dutch, because my boyfriend is Belgian.
items.e: want mijn vriend is Belg: verb in 2nd place in the second clause.

items.it: Marco is learning Dutch because he works in Ghent.
items.e: omdat hij in Gent werkt: the verb closes the subordinate clause.

items.it: We're taking the train, because the car is broken.
items.e: want + normal order: de auto is kapot.

items.it: The children are happy because it's vacation.
items.e: omdat het vakantie is: verb at the end.

subfirst.rule: If the sentence starts with a subordinate clause, that clause counts as 1st place: right after it comes the verb of the main clause, then the subject: Als het regent, blijf ik thuis. Verb – comma – verb. The subordinate clause is already in place.

items.it: If it rains, I'll stay home.
items.e: After the subordinate clause: blijf ik, not ik blijf as in English.

items.it: Since I'm sick, I'm not going to work.
items.e: The verb ga right after the comma, then the subject.

items.it: If you have time, we can have a coffee.
items.e: kunnen we after the subordinate clause, the infinitive drinken at the end.

items.it: When the weather is nice, we bike to the seaside.
items.e: Verb – comma – verb: is, fietsen.

items.it: When I'm tired, I go to bed early.
items.e: ga ik, then the infinitive slapen at the end.

items.it: Since the train is late, I'll arrive later.
items.e: After the subordinate clause, inversion: kom ik.

items.it: If you like, you can wait here. (formal)
items.e: kunt u after the comma, wachten at the end.

items.it: When he gets home, we'll eat together.
items.e: In the subordinate clause thuiskomt stays whole at the end; then eten we.

items.it: Since it's cold, I'm putting on my coat.
items.e: doe ik after the subordinate clause, the particle aan at the end.

items.it: When I'm in Bruges, I always eat fries.
items.e: eet ik, then altijd before the object.

rel.s: die/dat and the verb at the end
rel.rule: A relative clause starts with die (de words and plurals) or dat (het words) and has the verb at the end: de man die daar woont. It comes right after the word it refers to, and unlike English “who/that”, the relative pronoun can never be left out.

items.it: I have a friend who lives in Ghent.
items.e: een vriend is a de word → die; the verb woont at the end.

items.it: Do you know the girl who's standing over there?
items.e: het meisje → dat; staat at the end.

items.it: The woman who works there speaks Italian.
items.e: The relative clause sits inside the subject: werkt at the end of the relative clause, then the main verb spreekt.

items.it: I know a fry shop that makes really tasty fries.
items.e: de frituur → die; the verb maakt closes the relative clause.

items.it: The girl who lives next door to me is called Lotte.
items.e: dat … woont, then the main verb heet.

items.it: The train that goes to Brussels leaves at ten.
items.e: Subject + relative clause (verb gaat at the end), then vertrekt in 2nd place.

items.it: Is that the man you're looking for?
items.e: de man → die (required, even where English drops it); in the relative clause zoekt goes to the end.

items.it: The book I'm reading is really exciting.
items.e: het boek → dat; lees at the end of the relative clause, then is.

items.it: The people who live here are very friendly.
items.e: Plural → die; the verb wonen at the end of the relative clause.

items.it: My colleague who comes from Leuven speaks three languages.
items.e: die uit Leuven komt, then the main verb spreekt.

te.rule: After many verbs and expressions you use te + infinitive (like English “to”), always at the end: Het begint te regenen. For purpose (“in order to…”) use om … te: om brood te kopen. With a separable verb, te goes in the middle: op te staan.

items.it: It's starting to rain.
items.e: te regenen at the end, after the conjugated verb.

items.it: I'm trying to speak Dutch.
items.e: The object first, te spreken at the end.

items.it: I don't feel like cooking.
items.e: geen zin om … te koken: om opens, te + infinitive closes.

items.it: He's sitting in the garden reading.
items.e: zitten … te lezen: “to be (sitting) reading”; te lezen at the end.

items.it: Don't forget to call your mother.
items.e: Imperative first, te bellen at the end.

items.it: I don't have to work tomorrow.
items.e: niet hoeven te = not have to: te werken at the end.

items.it: I'm going to the bakery to buy bread.
items.e: Purpose: om brood te kopen; om at the start, te kopen at the end.

items.it: We don't have time to go to the movies.
items.e: Between om and te gaan comes the rest: naar de film.

items.it: She's saving money to buy a car.
items.e: om een auto te kopen: purpose, with te + infinitive at the end.

items.it: It's hard to get up early.
items.e: Separable verb: op te staan, with te in the middle, at the end.

cluster.rule: In a subordinate clause with two verbs, both go to the end: …omdat ik morgen moet werken, …dat hij is gekomen. The order of the two verbs is free: werken moet and gekomen is are just as correct.

items.it: I think he came.
items.e: is gekomen or gekomen is: both at the end.

items.it: I hope you can come.
items.e: Modal and infinitive together at the end of the subordinate clause.

items.it: She knows I have to work tomorrow.
items.e: morgen stays before the two verbs: moet werken / werken moet.

items.it: I don't know if he wants to come.
items.e: After of the two verbs go to the end.

items.it: Marc says he's been sick.
items.e: ziek first, then is geweest / geweest is.

items.it: I'm glad you came.
items.e: Auxiliary and participle together at the end, in either order.

items.it: Do you know if the train has already left?
items.e: al before the final verb group.

items.it: My mother says she has moved to Leuven.
items.e: The place first, the two verbs at the end.

items.it: I think we've missed the bus.
items.e: Object first, then hebben gemist / gemist hebben.

items.it: The children are happy because they're allowed to swim.
items.e: After omdat: mogen zwemmen or zwemmen mogen, always at the end.
